walkthroughs.body_html:
Coordinate Systems & Time — a core area of A-Level Astronomy.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Coordinate Systems & Time brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Coordinate Systems & Time.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Right ascension is the celestial equivalent of:
options: Latitude
Longitude
Altitude
Azimuth

mcqs.q: Declination is measured in degrees north or south of the:
options: Horizon
Celestial equator
Ecliptic
Observer's meridian

mcqs.q: The ecliptic is tilted to the celestial equator by about:
options: 0 degrees
23.5 degrees
45 degrees
90 degrees

mcqs.q: Local sidereal time equals the right ascension of an object that is:
options: On the horizon
On the observer's meridian
Always at the zenith
Currently setting

mcqs.q: Does a star's right ascension change through the night like clock time?
options: Yes, RA changes every hour like a clock.
RA depends on where you stand on Earth.
No - it stays essentially fixed; RA and declination are nearly constant for a star.
Because of the Moon's gravitational pull.

mcqs.q: What does declination correspond to on Earth?
options: RA depends on where you stand on Earth.
Latitude - degrees north or south of the celestial equator.
Longitude.
Altitude above the horizon.

mcqs.q: Why is the ecliptic tilted to the celestial equator?
options: Because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees.
Because the Sun orbits at an angle by chance.
RA depends on where you stand on Earth.
Because of the Moon's gravitational pull.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Declination”?
options: Time kept by the apparent motion of the stars; the local sidereal time equals the right ascension of an object currently on the meridian.
The apparent yearly path of the Sun across the celestial sphere, tilted about 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator because of Earth's axial tilt.
The angle, measured westward, between an object's current position and the observer's meridian, showing how long since it crossed the meridian.
The celestial equivalent of latitude, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator, fixing an object's position together with right ascension.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Right ascension”?
options: The projection of the Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere, the reference circle from which declination is measured.
The angle, measured westward, between an object's current position and the observer's meridian, showing how long since it crossed the meridian.
The celestial equivalent of longitude, measured eastward along the celestial equator in hours, minutes and seconds from the vernal equinox.
The apparent yearly path of the Sun across the celestial sphere, tilted about 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator because of Earth's axial tilt.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Celestial equator”?
options: The angle, measured westward, between an object's current position and the observer's meridian, showing how long since it crossed the meridian.
The projection of the Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere, the reference circle from which declination is measured.
The celestial equivalent of longitude, measured eastward along the celestial equator in hours, minutes and seconds from the vernal equinox.
The celestial equivalent of latitude, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator, fixing an object's position together with right ascension.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Ecliptic”?
options: The apparent yearly path of the Sun across the celestial sphere, tilted about 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator because of Earth's axial tilt.
Time kept by the apparent motion of the stars; the local sidereal time equals the right ascension of an object currently on the meridian.
The angle, measured westward, between an object's current position and the observer's meridian, showing how long since it crossed the meridian.
The celestial equivalent of latitude, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator, fixing an object's position together with right ascension.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Sidereal time”?
options: The projection of the Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere, the reference circle from which declination is measured.
The celestial equivalent of longitude, measured eastward along the celestial equator in hours, minutes and seconds from the vernal equinox.
The apparent yearly path of the Sun across the celestial sphere, tilted about 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator because of Earth's axial tilt.
Time kept by the apparent motion of the stars; the local sidereal time equals the right ascension of an object currently on the meridian.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Hour angle”?
options: The apparent yearly path of the Sun across the celestial sphere, tilted about 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator because of Earth's axial tilt.
The projection of the Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere, the reference circle from which declination is measured.
The angle, measured westward, between an object's current position and the observer's meridian, showing how long since it crossed the meridian.
Time kept by the apparent motion of the stars; the local sidereal time equals the right ascension of an object currently on the meridian.

0 degrees
